**PSR study finds mandatory reimbursement cut APP fraud losses by £73 million**

*An independent review commissioned by the Payment Systems Regulator provides the first quantified evidence that the UK's mandatory APP fraud reimbursement policy is reducing fraud, not just shifting costs.*

The PSR published findings from Frontier Economics on July 1 showing that authorised push payment fraud losses fell by an estimated £73 million annually since the mandatory reimbursement requirement took effect. The study found a 97% refund rate across covered transactions, suggesting the policy has created meaningful financial incentives for sending banks to invest in fraud prevention.

The result complicates the narrative that had been building around reimbursement costs. Monzo's 85% surge in fraud reimbursement spending, reported in May, led several industry voices to question whether the policy was sustainable. The Frontier Economics analysis suggests the regime is functioning as intended: by making banks bear the cost of fraud they fail to prevent, it has driven behavioural change in how firms screen outbound payments.

The PSR said it would launch a consultation on the scheme's next phase, though it did not specify the scope. For banks still calibrating their fraud prevention investment, the message is clear: the regulator now has evidence the policy works and is unlikely to soften its approach.

*Sources: [Forcing banks to refund some scam victims 'cut payment fraud by £73 million'](https://www.moneysavingexpert.com/news/2026/07/push-payment-fraud-consultation/) — MoneySavingExpert | [Payment fraud falls by £73m following PSR reimbursement scheme](https://www.regulationtomorrow.com/2026/07/payment-fraud-falls-by-73m-following-psr-reimbursement-scheme/) — Regulation Tomorrow | [UK Payment Fraud Drops by £73m as PSR Reimbursement Scheme Drives 97% Refund Rate](https://ffnews.com/news/uk-payment-fraud-drops-by-73m-as-psr-reimbursement-scheme-drives-97-refund-rate) — Fintech Finance News*

**Greece's IRIS goes live with cross-border instant transfers via EuroPA network**

*Greek instant payment service IRIS has launched cross-border transfers across Europe using mobile numbers, marking the first live use of the EuroPA interoperability framework connecting national account-to-account schemes.*

IRIS, Greece's domestic instant payment system, now enables cross-border money transfers across Europe using only the recipient's mobile number. The service operates through EuroPA, a network that connects national account-to-account instant payment solutions such as Portugal's MB WAY and Greece's IRIS Payments. The launch follows Greece's connection to the wider European instant payments network, covered on July 1.

EuroPA sits alongside rather than within the EPI/Wero infrastructure, offering an alternative interoperability path for national schemes that want cross-border reach without full integration into EPI. For countries whose domestic instant payment schemes predate or sit outside EPI, this provides a route to pan-European reach that preserves their existing rails.

The practical test will be volume. Cross-border person-to-person payments within Europe remain overwhelmingly card-based, and shifting that traffic to account-to-account rails requires both consumer trust and merchant acceptance that mobile-number-based transfers can match the convenience of existing options.

*Sources: [IRIS launches instant cross-border money transfers across Europe using only mobile numbers](https://www.naftemporiki.gr/english/2131636/iris-launches-instant-cross-border-money-transfers-across-europe-using-only-mobile-numbers/) — Naftemporiki | [IRIS Launches Instant Cross-Border Money Transfers Across Europe via Mobile Numbers](https://indicator.gr/iris-launches-instant-cross-border-money-transfers-across-europe-via-mobile-numbers?amp=1) — Indicator*

**Lightspark secures Europe's first combined MiCA and e-money licence in Estonia**

*Lightspark Payments Europe has received both a crypto-asset service provider authorisation under MiCA and an electronic money institution licence from Estonia's financial supervisor, positioning it to offer regulated crypto payment services across the EU.*

Lightspark, the payments company founded by former Meta executive David Marcus, announced on July 2 that its European subsidiary has been authorised by Estonia's Finantsinspektsioon as both a crypto-asset service provider under MiCA and an electronic money institution. The dual licence allows it to issue e-money and provide crypto-asset services from a single regulated entity, passportable across the EU.

The company has been building payment infrastructure around Bitcoin's Lightning Network and stablecoins. Holding both licences from a single regulator simplifies its ability to bridge fiat and crypto payment flows, a capability that becomes commercially relevant as stablecoin settlement gains traction. Mastercard's recent addition of stablecoin settlement to its merchant network and the Open USD launch backed by Visa, Mastercard and Google both point to growing institutional demand for this bridging layer.

Estonia has been among the more permissive EU member states for crypto licensing, though its regulator tightened requirements significantly in recent years. That Lightspark chose Estonia for its MiCA base suggests the jurisdiction retains advantages for firms seeking rapid authorisation within the new framework.

*Sources: [Lightspark becomes first payments company in Estonia to get MiCA licence](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/110322/lightspark-becomes-first-payments-company-in-estonia-to-get-mica-licence) — Finextra*

**Pay.UK introduces flexible liquidity model for Faster Payments access**

*Pay.UK's new liquidity framework for Faster Payments allows participants to choose how they fund settlement, removing a structural barrier that has limited direct access to UK instant payment rails.*

Pay.UK has launched a flexible liquidity model that gives Faster Payments participants a choice in how they pre-fund settlement obligations. The change addresses a long-standing complaint from smaller banks and non-bank payment service providers that the fixed liquidity requirements for direct participation were disproportionate to their transaction volumes, effectively forcing them to access the system indirectly through sponsor banks.

The reform sits within a broader programme of infrastructure modernisation. The UK government's consultation on next-generation retail payments infrastructure, launched in late June, and the recent launch of the UK Payments Initiative as a domestic alternative to card scheme rails, both depend on widening direct access to faster payment systems. A liquidity model that scales with a participant's actual usage rather than imposing a flat requirement makes direct access commercially viable for a larger set of firms.

For fintechs and challenger banks that have built their real-time payment capabilities through agency arrangements, the practical question is whether the new model shifts the economics enough to justify the operational investment of direct participation. The answer will vary by firm, but the structural barrier is now lower.

*Sources: [Pay.UK introduces flexible liquidity model for Faster Payments access](https://www.finextra.com/) — referenced from previously covered list, July 1*
